entries.0540b514a57f9d4d84b0b7cf8ead50aea538303f: <div sID="gen11180" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="44" osisID="Ps.44" sID="Ps.44"/> <div eID="gen11180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11181" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11182" type="x-p"/> We are not told either who was the penmen of this psalm or when and upon what occasion it was penned, upon a melancholy occasion, we are sure, not so much to the penman himself (then we could have found occasions enough for it in the history of David and his afflictions), but to the church of God in general; and therefore, if we suppose it penned by David, yet we must attribute it purely to the Spirit of prophecy, and must conclude that the Spirit (whatever he himself had) had in view the captivity of Babylon, or the sufferings of the Jewish church under Antiochus, or rather the afflicted state of the Christian church in its early days (to which <reference osisRef="Ps.44.22">ver. 22</reference> is applied by the apostle, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.36">Rom. viii. 36</reference>), and indeed in all its days on earth, for it is its determined lot that it must enter into the kingdom of heaven through many tribulations. And, if we have any gospel-psalms pointing at the privileges and comforts of Christians, why should we not have one pointing at their trials and exercises? It is a psalm calculated for a day of fasting and humiliation upon occasion of some public calamity, either pressing or threatening. In it the church is taught, I. To own with thankfulness, to the glory of God, the great things God has done for their fathers, <reference osisRef="Ps.44.1-Ps.44.8">ver. 1-8</reference>. II. To exhibit a memorial of their present calamitous estate, <reference osisRef="Ps.44.9-Ps.44.16">ver. 9-16</reference>. III. To file a protestation of their integrity and adherence to God notwithstanding, <reference osisRef="Ps.44.17-Ps.44.22">ver. 17-22</reference>. IV. To lodge a petition at the throne of grace for succour and relief, <reference osisRef="Ps.44.22-Ps.44.26">ver. 22-26</reference>. In singing this psalm we ought to give God the praise of what he has formerly done for his people, to represent our own grievances, or sympathize with those parts of the church that are in distress, to engage ourselves, whatever happens, to cleave to God and duty, and then cheerfully to wait the event.
entries.bbe43c3aeb577432b097f6b4154396082c27d425: <div eID="gen11182" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11181" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Grateful Acknowledgment of Past Mercies; Consecration to God.</title> <div sID="gen11183" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> We have heard with our ears, O God, our fathers have told us, <hi type="italic">what</hi> work thou didst in their days, in the times of old. <hi type="super">2</hi> <hi type="italic">How</hi> thou didst drive out the heathen with thy hand, and plantedst them; <hi type="italic">how</hi> thou didst afflict the people, and cast them out. <hi type="super">3</hi> For they got not the land in possession by their own sword, neither did their own arm save them: but thy right hand, and thine arm, and the light of thy countenance, because thou hadst a favour unto them. <hi type="super">4</hi> Thou art my King, O God: command deliverances for Jacob. <hi type="super">5</hi> Through thee will we push down our enemies: through thy name will we tread them under that rise up against us. <hi type="super">6</hi> For I will not trust in my bow, neither shall my sword save me. <hi type="super">7</hi> But thou hast saved us from our enemies, and hast put them to shame that hated us. <hi type="super">8</hi> In God we boast all the day long, and praise thy name for ever. Selah. <div eID="gen11183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11184" type="x-p"/> Some observe that most of the psalms that are entitled <hi type="italic">Maschil—psalms of instruction,</hi> are sorrowful psalms; for afflictions give instructions, and sorrow of spirit opens the ear to them. <hi type="italic">Blessed is the man whom thou chastenest and teachest.</hi> <div eID="gen11184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11185" type="x-p"/> In these verses the church, though now trampled upon, calls to remembrance the days of her triumph, of her triumph in God and over her enemies. This is very largely mentioned here, 1. As an aggravation of the present distress. The yoke of servitude cannot but lie very heavily on the necks of those that used to wear the crown of victory; and the tokens of God's displeasure must needs be most grievous to those that have been long accustomed to the tokens of his favour. 2. As an encouragement to hope that God would yet turn again their captivity and return in mercy to them; accordingly he mixes prayers and comfortable expectations with his record of former mercies. Observe, <div eID="gen11185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11186" type="x-p"/> I. Their commemoration of the great things God had formerly done for them. <div eID="gen11186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11187" type="x-p"/> 1. In general (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Our fathers have told us what work thou didst in their days.</hi> Observe, (1.) The many operations of providence are here spoken of as one work—"They have told us the <hi type="italic">work</hi> which thou didst;" for there is a wonderful harmony and uniformity in all that God does, and the many wheels make but one wheel (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.13">Ezek. x. 13</reference>), many works make but one work. (2.) It is a debt which every age owes to posterity to keep an account of God's works of wonder, and to transmit the knowledge of them to the next generation. Those that went before us told us what God did in their days, we are bound to tell those that come after us what he has done in our days, and let them do the like justice to those that shall succeed them; thus shall <hi type="italic">one generation praise his works to another</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.4">Ps. cxlv. 4</reference>), the <hi type="italic">fathers to the children shall make known his truth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.38.19">Isa. xxxviii. 19</reference>. (3.) We must not only make mention of the work God has done in our own days, but must also acquaint ourselves and our children with what he did in the times of old, long before our own days; and of this we have in the scripture a sure word of history, as sure as the word of prophecy. (4.) Children must diligently attend to what their parents tell them of the wonderful works of God, and keep it in remembrance, as that which will be of great use to them. (5.) Former experiences of God's power and goodness are strong supports to faith and powerful pleas in prayer under present calamities. See how Gideon insists upon it (<reference osisRef="Judg.6.13">Judg. vi. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Where are all his miracles which our fathers told us of?</hi> <div eID="gen11187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11188" type="x-p"/> 2. In particular, their fathers had told them, <div eID="gen11188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11189" type="x-p"/> (1.) How wonderfully God planted Israel in Canaan at first, <reference osisRef="Ps.44.2-Ps.44.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. He drove out the natives, to make room for Israel, afflicted them, and cast them out, gave them as dust to Israel's sword and as driven stubble to their bow. The many complete victories which Israel obtained over the Canaanites, under the command of Joshua, were not to be attributed to themselves, nor could they challenge the glory of them. [1.] They were not owing to their own merit, but to God's favour and free grace: It was <hi type="italic">through the light of thy countenance, because thou hadst a favour to them. Not for thy righteousness, or the uprightness of thy heart, doth God drive them out from before thee</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.5-Deut.9.6">Deut. ix. 5, 6</reference>), but because God would <hi type="italic">perform the oath which he swore unto their fathers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.7.8">Deut. vii. 8</reference>. The less praise this allows us the more comfort it administers to us, that we may see all our successes and enlargements coming to us from the favour of God and the light of his countenance. [2.] They were not owing to their own might, but to God's power engaged for them, without which all their own efforts and endeavours would have been fruitless. It was not by their own sword that they got the land in possession, though they had great numbers of mighty men; nor did their own arm save them from being driven back by the Canaanites and put to shame; but it was God's <hi type="italic">right hand</hi> and his <hi type="italic">arm.</hi> He fought for Israel, else they would have fought in vain; it was through him that they did valiantly and victoriously. It was God that planted Israel in that good land, as the careful husbandman plants a tree, from which he promises himself fruit. See <reference osisRef="Ps.80.8">Ps. lxxx. 8</reference>. This is applicable to the planting of the Christian church in the world, by the preaching of the gospel. Paganism was wonderfully driven out, as the Canaanites, not all at once, but by little and little, not by any human policy or power (for God chose to do it by the weak and foolish things of the world), but by the wisdom and power of God—Christ by his Spirit went forth conquering and to conquer; and the remembrance of that is a great support and comfort to those that groan under the yoke of antichristian tyranny, for to the state of the church under the power of the New-Testament Babylon, some think (and particularly the learned Amyraldus), the complaints in the latter part of this psalm may very fitly be accommodated. He that by his power and goodness planted a church for himself in the world will certainly support it by the same power and goodness; and the <hi type="italic">gates of hell shall not prevail against it.</hi> <div eID="gen11189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11190" type="x-p"/> (2.) How frequently he had given them success against their enemies that attempted to disturb them in the possession of that good land (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou hast,</hi> many a time, <hi type="italic">saved us from our enemies,</hi> and hast put to flight, and so put to shame, <hi type="italic">those that hated us,</hi> witness the successes of the judges against the nations that oppressed Israel. Many a time have the persecutors of the Christian church, and those that hate it, been put to shame by the power of truth, <reference osisRef="Acts.6.10">Acts vi. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen11190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11191" type="x-p"/> II. The good use they make of this record, and had formerly made of it, in consideration of the great things God had done for their fathers of old. <div eID="gen11191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11192" type="x-p"/> 1. They had taken God for their sovereign Lord, had sworn allegiance to him, and put themselves under his protection (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou art my King, O God!</hi> He speaks in the name of the church, as (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.12">Ps. lxxiv. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">Thou art my King of old.</hi> God, as a king, has made laws for his church, provided for the peace and good order of it, judged for it, pleaded its cause, fought its battles, and protected it; it is his kingdom in the world, and ought to be subject to him, and to pay him tribute. Or the psalmist speaks for himself here: "Lord, <hi type="italic">Thou art my King;</hi> whither shall I go with my petitions, but to thee? The favour I ask is not for myself, but for thy church." Note, It is every one's duty to improve his personal interest at the throne of grace for the public welfare and prosperity of the people of God; as Moses, "<hi type="italic">If I have found grace in thy sight,</hi> guide thy people," <reference osisRef="Exod.33.13">Exod. xxxiii. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen11192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11193" type="x-p"/> 2. They had always applied to him by prayer for deliverance when at any time they were in distress: <hi type="italic">Command deliverances for Jacob.</hi> Observe, (1.) The enlargedness of their desire. They pray for deliverances, not one, but many, as many as they had need of, how many soever they were, a series of deliverances, a deliverance from every danger. (2.) The strength of their faith in the power of God. They do not say, <hi type="italic">Work deliverances,</hi> but <hi type="italic">Command them,</hi> which denotes his doing it easily and instantly—<hi type="italic">Speak and it is done</hi> (such was the faith of the centurion, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.8">Matt. viii. 8</reference>, <hi type="italic">Speak the word only, and my servant shall be healed</hi>); it denotes also his doing it effectually: "Command it, as one having authority, whose command will be obeyed." <hi type="italic">Where the word of a king is there is power,</hi> much more the word of the King of kings. <div eID="gen11193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11194" type="x-p"/> 3. They had trusted and triumphed in him. As they owned it was not their own sword and bow that had saved them (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.3">v. 3</reference>), so neither did they trust to their own sword or bow to save them for the future (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will not trust in my bow,</hi> nor in any of my military preparations, as if those would stand me in stead without God. No; <hi type="italic">through thee will we push down our enemies</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.5">v. 5</reference>); we will attempt it in thy strength, relying only upon that, and not upon the number or valour of our forces; and, having thee on our side, we will not doubt of success in the attempt. <hi type="italic">Through thy name</hi> (by virtue of thy wisdom directing us, thy power strengthening us and working for us, and thy promise securing success to us) we shall, we <hi type="italic">will, tread those under that rise up against us.</hi>" <div eID="gen11194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11195" type="x-p"/> 4. They had made him their joy and praise (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.8">v. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">In God we have boasted;</hi> in him we do and will boast, every day, and all the day long." When their enemies boasted of their strength and successes, as Sennacherib and Rabshakeh hectored Hezekiah, they owned they had nothing to boast of, in answer thereunto, but their relation to God and their interest in him; and, if he were for them, they could set all the world at defiance. <hi type="italic">Let him that glories glory in the Lord,</hi> and let that for ever exclude all other boasting. Let those that trust in God make their boast in him, for they know whom they have trusted; let them <hi type="italic">boast in him all the day long,</hi> for it is a subject that can never be exhausted. But let them withal <hi type="italic">praise his name for ever;</hi> if they have the comfort of his name, let them give unto him the glory due to it.
entries.7add488c407e359bb86713e9919cc96d01b1fb5c: <div eID="gen11195" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Afflicted Condition of Israel.</title> <div sID="gen11196" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> But thou hast cast off, and put us to shame; and goest not forth with our armies. <hi type="super">10</hi> Thou makest us to turn back from the enemy: and they which hate us spoil for themselves. <hi type="super">11</hi> Thou hast given us like sheep <hi type="italic">appointed</hi> for meat; and hast scattered us among the heathen. 12 Thou sellest thy people for nought, and dost not increase <hi type="italic">thy wealth</hi> by their price. <hi type="super">13</hi> Thou makest us a reproach to our neighbours, a scorn and a derision to them that are round about us. <hi type="super">14</hi> Thou makest us a byword among the heathen, a shaking of the head among the people. <hi type="super">15</hi> My confusion <hi type="italic">is</hi> continually before me, and the shame of my face hath covered me, <hi type="super">16</hi> For the voice of him that reproacheth and blasphemeth; by reason of the enemy and avenger. <div eID="gen11196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11197" type="x-p"/> The people of God here complain to him of the low and afflicted condition that they were now in, under the prevailing power of their enemies and oppressors, which was the more grievous to them because <hi type="italic">they</hi> were now trampled upon, who had always been used, in their struggles with their neighbours, to win the day and get the upper hand, and because those were now their oppressors whom they had many a time triumphed over and made tributaries, and especially because they had boasted in their God with great assurance that he would still protect and prosper them, which made the distress they were in, and the disgrace they were under, the more shameful. Let us see what the complaint is. <div eID="gen11197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11198" type="x-p"/> I. That they wanted the usual tokens of God's favour to them and presence with them (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou hast cast off;</hi> thou seemest to have cast us off and our cause, and to have cast off thy wonted care of us and concern for us, and so hast put us to shame, for we boasted of the constancy and perpetuity of thy favour. Our armies go forth as usual, but they are put to flight; we gain no ground, but lose what we have gained, for thou goest not forth with them, for, if thou didst, which way soever they turned they would prosper; but it is quite contrary." Note, God's people, when they are cast down, are tempted to think themselves cast off and forsaken of God; but it is a mistake. <hi type="italic">Hath God cast away his people? God forbid,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.1">Rom. xi. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen11198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11199" type="x-p"/> II. That they were put to the worst before their enemies in the field of battle (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou makest us to turn back from the enemy,</hi> as Joshua complained when they met with a repulse at Ai (<reference osisRef="Josh.7.8">Josh. vii. 8</reference>): "We are dispirited, and have lost the ancient valour of Israelites; we flee, we fall, before those that used to flee and fall before us; and then those that hate us have the plunder of our camp and of our country; they spoil for themselves, and reckon all their own that they can lay their hands on. Attempts to shake off the Babylonish yoke have been ineffectual, and we have rather lost ground by them." <div eID="gen11199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11200" type="x-p"/> III. That they were doomed to the sword and to captivity (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.11">v. 11</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou hast given us like sheep appointed for meat.</hi> They make no more scruple of killing an Israelite than of killing a sheep; nay, like the butcher, they make a trade of it, they take a pleasure in it as a hungry man in his meat; and we are led with as much ease, and as little resistance, as a lamb to the slaughter; many are slain, and the rest scattered among the heathen, continually insulted by their malice or in danger of being infected by their iniquities." They looked upon themselves as bought and sold, and charged it upon God, <hi type="italic">Thou sellest thy people,</hi> when they should have charged it upon their own sin. <hi type="italic">For your iniquities have you sold yourselves,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.50.1">Isa. l. 1</reference>. However, thus far was right that they looked above the instruments of their trouble and kept their eye upon God, as well knowing that their worst enemies had no power against them <hi type="italic">but what was given them from above;</hi> they own it was God that <hi type="italic">delivered them into the hand of the ungodly,</hi> as that which is sold is delivered to the buyer. <hi type="italic">Thou sellest them for nought, and dost not increase in their price</hi> (so it may be read); "thou dost not sell them by auction, to those that will bid most for them, but in haste, to those that will bid first for them; any one shall have them that will." Or, as we read it, <hi type="italic">Thou dost not increase thy wealth by their price,</hi> intimating that they could have suffered this contentedly if they had been sure that it would redound to the glory of God and that his interest might be some way served by their sufferings; but it was quite contrary: Israel's disgrace turned to God's dishonour, so that he was so far from being a gainer in his glory by the sale of them that it should seem he was greatly a loser by it; see <reference osisRef="Isa.52.5">Isa. lii. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.20">Ezek. xxxvi. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen11200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11201" type="x-p"/> IV. That they were loaded with contempt, and all possible ignominy was put upon them. In this also they acknowledge God: "<hi type="italic">Thou makest us a reproach;</hi> thou bringest those calamities upon us which occasion the reproach, and thou permittest their virulent tongues to smite us." They complain, 1. That they were ridiculed and bantered, and were looked upon as the most contemptible people under the sun; their troubles were turned to their reproach, and upon the account of them they were derided. 2. That their neighbours, those about them, from whom they could not withdraw, were most abusive to them, <reference osisRef="Ps.44.13">v. 13</reference>. 3. That the heathen, the people that were strangers to the commonwealth of Israel and aliens to the covenants of promise, made them a by-word, and shook the head at them, as triumphing in their fall, <reference osisRef="Ps.44.14">v. 14</reference>. 4. That the reproach was constant and incessant (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">My confusion is continually before me.</hi> The church in general, the psalmist in particular, were continually teased and vexed with the insults of the enemy. Concerning those that are going down every one cries, "Down with them." 5. That it was very grievous, and in a manner overwhelmed him: <hi type="italic">The shame of my face has covered me.</hi> He blushed for sin, or rather for the dishonour done to God, and then it was a holy blushing. 6. That it reflected upon God himself; the reproach which the enemy and the avenger cast upon them was downright blasphemy against God, <reference osisRef="Ps.44.16">v. 16</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.3">2 Kings xix. 3</reference>. There was therefore strong reason to believe that God would appear for them. As there is no trouble more grievous to a generous and ingenuous mind than reproach and calumny, so there is none more grievous to a holy gracious soul than blasphemy and dishonour done to God.
entries.c8752ff530ffb4b4e443af5bcbbe6caad950707c: <div eID="gen11201" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Israel's Appeal to God.</title> <div sID="gen11202" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> All this is come upon us; yet have we not forgotten thee, neither have we dealt falsely in thy covenant. 18 Our heart is not turned back, neither have our steps declined from thy way; <hi type="super">19</hi> Though thou hast sore broken us in the place of dragons, and covered us with the shadow of death. 20 If we have forgotten the name of our God, or stretched out our hands to a strange god; <hi type="super">21</hi> Shall not God search this out? for he knoweth the secrets of the heart. <hi type="super">22</hi> Yea, for thy sake are we killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter. <hi type="super">23</hi> Awake, why sleepest thou, O Lord? arise, cast <hi type="italic">us</hi> not off for ever. <hi type="super">24</hi> Wherefore hidest thou thy face, <hi type="italic">and</hi> forgettest our affliction and our oppression? <hi type="super">25</hi> For our soul is bowed down to the dust: our belly cleaveth unto the earth. <hi type="super">26</hi> Arise for our help, and redeem us for thy mercies' sake. <div eID="gen11202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11203" type="x-p"/> The people of God, being greatly afflicted and oppressed, here apply to him; whither else should they go? <div eID="gen11203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11204" type="x-p"/> I. By way of appeal, concerning their integrity, which he only is an infallible judge of, and which he will certainly be the rewarder of. Two things they call God to witness to:— <div eID="gen11204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11205" type="x-p"/> 1. That, though they suffered these hard things, yet they kept close to God and to their duty (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.17">v. 17</reference>): "<hi type="italic">All this has come upon us,</hi> and it is as bad perhaps as bad can be, <hi type="italic">yet have we not forgotten thee,</hi> neither cast off the thoughts of thee nor deserted the worship of thee; for, though we cannot deny but that we have dealt foolishly, yet we have not <hi type="italic">dealt falsely in thy covenant,</hi> so as to cast thee off and take to other gods. Though idolaters were our conquerors, we did not therefore entertain any more favourable thoughts of their idols and idolatries; though thou hast seemed to forsake us and withdraw from us, yet we have not therefore forsaken thee." The trouble they had been long in was very great: "We have been <hi type="italic">sorely broken in the place of dragons,</hi> among men as fierce, and furious, and cruel, as dragons. We have been <hi type="italic">covered with the shadow of death,</hi> that is, we have been under deep melancholy and apprehensive of nothing short of death. We have been wrapped up in obscurity, and buried alive; and thou hast thus broken us, thou hast thus covered us (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.19">v. 19</reference>), yet we have not harboured any hard thoughts of thee, nor meditated a retreat from thy service. Though thou hast slain us, we have continued to trust in thee: <hi type="italic">Our heart has not turned back;</hi> we have not secretly withdrawn our affections from thee, neither have our steps, either in our religious worship or in our conversation, <hi type="italic">declined from thy way</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.18">v. 18</reference>), the way which thou hast appointed us to walk in." When the heart turns back the steps will soon decline; for it is the evil heart of unbelief that inclines to depart from God. Note, We may the better bear our troubles, how pressing soever, if in them we still hold fast our integrity. While our troubles do not drive us from our duty to God we should not suffer them to drive us from our comfort in God; for he will not leave us if we do not leave him. For the proof of their integrity they take God's omniscience to witness, which is as much the comfort of the upright in heart as it is the terror of hypocrites (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.20-Ps.44.21">v. 20, 21</reference>): "<hi type="italic">If we have forgotten the name of our God,</hi> under pretence that he had forgotten us, or in our distress have <hi type="italic">stretched out our hands to a strange god,</hi> as more likely to help us, <hi type="italic">shall not God search this out?</hi> Shall he not know it more fully and distinctly than we know that which we have with the greatest care and diligence searched out? Shall he not judge it, and call us to an account for it?" Forgetting God was a heart-sin, and stretching our the hand to a strange god was often a secret sin, <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.12">Ezek. viii. 12</reference>. But heart-sins and secret sins are known to God, and must be reckoned for; for <hi type="italic">he knows the secrets of the heart,</hi> and therefore is a infallible judge of the words and actions. <div eID="gen11205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11206" type="x-p"/> 2. That they suffered these hard things because they kept close to God and to their duty (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.22">v. 22</reference>): "It is <hi type="italic">for thy sake that we are killed all the day long,</hi> because we stand related to thee, are called by thy name, call upon thy name, and will not worship other gods." In this the Spirit of prophecy had reference to those who suffered even unto death for the testimony of Christ, to whom it is applied, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.36">Rom. viii. 36</reference>. So many were killed, and put to such lingering deaths, that they were in the killing all the day long; so universally was this practised that when a man became a Christian he reckoned himself as a <hi type="italic">sheep appointed for the slaughter.</hi> <div eID="gen11206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11207" type="x-p"/> II. By way of petition, with reference to their present distress, that God would, in his own due time, work deliverance for them. 1. Their request is very importunate: <hi type="italic">Awake, arise,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.44.23">v. 23</reference>. <hi type="italic">Arise for our help; redeem us</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.26">v. 26</reference>); come speedily and powerfully to our relief, <reference osisRef="Ps.80.2">Ps. lxxx. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">Stir up thy strength, and come and save us.</hi> They had complained (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.12">v. 12</reference>) that God had sold them; here they pray (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.26">v. 26</reference>) that God would redeem them; for there is no appealing from God, but by appealing to him. If he sell us, it is not any one else that can redeem us; the same hand that tears must heal, that smites must bind up, <reference osisRef="Hos.6.1">Hos. vi. 1</reference>. They had complained (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.9">v. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">Thou hast cast us off;</hi> but here they pray (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.23">v. 23</reference>), "<hi type="italic">Cast us not off forever;</hi> let us not be finally forsaken of God." 2. The expostulations are very moving: <hi type="italic">Why sleepest thou?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.44.23">v. 23</reference>. He that keeps Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps; but, when he does not immediately appear for the deliverance of his people, they are tempted to think he sleeps. The expression is figurative (as <reference osisRef="Ps.78.65">Ps. lxxviii. 65</reference>, <hi type="italic">Then the Lord awaked as one out of sleep</hi>); but it was applicable to Christ in the letter (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.24">Matt. viii. 24</reference>); he was asleep when his disciples were in a storm, and they awoke him, saying, <hi type="italic">Lord, save us, we perish. "Wherefore hidest thou thy face,</hi> that we may not see thee and the light of thy countenance?" Or, "that thou mayest not see us and our distresses? Thou forgettest our affliction and our oppression, for it still continues, and we see no way open for our deliverance." And, 3. The pleas are very proper, not their own merit and righteousness, though they had the testimony of their consciences concerning their integrity, but they plead the poor sinner's pleas. (1.) Their own misery, which made them the proper objects of the divine compassion (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.25">v. 25</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Our soul is bowed down to the dust</hi> under prevailing grief and fear. We have become as creeping things, the most despicable animals: <hi type="italic">Our belly cleaves unto the earth;</hi> we cannot lift up ourselves, neither revive our own drooping spirits nor recover ourselves out of our low and sad condition, and we lie exposed to be trodden on by every insulting foe." 2. God's mercy: "<hi type="italic">O redeem us for they mercies' sake;</hi> we depend upon the goodness of thy nature, which is the glory of thy name (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.6">Exod. xxxiv. 6</reference>), and upon those sure mercies of David which are conveyed by the covenant to all his spiritual seed."  <chapter eID="Ps.44"/> <div eID="gen11207" type="x-p"/>

entries.7895533817181d72a13eed1fdcf5ee24e01c2672: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5966"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 44</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.44.1-Ps.44.26">Psa 44:1-26</reference>. In a time of great national distress, probably in David's reign, the Psalmist recounts God's gracious dealings in former times, and the confidence they had learned to repose in Him. After a vivid picture of their calamities, he humbly expostulates against God's apparent forgetfulness, reminding Him of their faithfulness and mourning their heavy sorrows.</title> <div sID="gen9085" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5966"/>1-3. This period is that of the settlement of Canaan (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.12">Jos 24:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.6.3">Jud 6:3</reference>).<div eID="gen9085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9086" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have told--</hi>or, "related" (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.10.2">Ex 10:2</reference>). <div eID="gen9086" type="x-p"/>
entries.f519a87d0072a65e0f31c0ae4921887f47a52a2f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5968"/><div sID="gen9088" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5968"/><hi type="bold">4. Thou art my King--</hi>literally, "he who is my King," sustaining the same covenant relation as to the "fathers." <div eID="gen9088" type="x-p"/>
entries.f83974c9647312e1e525ec6668cbe6e6fa1fb28d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5969"/><div sID="gen9089" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5969"/>5. The figure drawn from the habits of the ox. <div eID="gen9089" type="x-p"/>
entries.35a68093659bfa7382b86e39c67cfffe66b62e41: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5970"/><div sID="gen9090" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5970"/>6-8. God is not only our sole help, but only worthy of praise. <div eID="gen9090" type="x-p"/>
entries.73df1170fe56791163724b7938c033098e0eeb30: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5973"/><div sID="gen9093" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5973"/><hi type="bold">9. But--</hi>contrasting, cast off as abhorrent (<reference osisRef="Ps.43.2">Psa 43:2</reference>).<div eID="gen9093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9094" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">goest not forth--</hi>literally, "will not go" (<reference osisRef="2Sam.5.23">2Sa 5:23</reference>). In several consecutive verses the leading verb is future, and the following one past (in Hebrew), thus denoting the causes and effects. Thus (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.10-Ps.44.12">Psa 44:10-12</reference>), when defeated, spoiling follows; when delivered as sheep, dispersion follows, &c. <div eID="gen9094" type="x-p"/>
entries.3459afdf197008213e18d88c0591ed0046ceb1f2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5974"/><div sID="gen9095" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5974"/>11. The Babylonian captivity not necessarily meant. There were others (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.46">1Ki 8:46</reference>). <div eID="gen9095" type="x-p"/>
entries.d800ed181bd4cc77501c2fca90fd4edce69e9f0e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5975"/><div sID="gen9096" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5975"/>13-14. (Compare <reference osisRef="Deut.28.37">De 28:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.79.4">Psa 79:4</reference>). <div eID="gen9096" type="x-p"/>
entries.39cb272a28a8b4dcd5be0b26402aee9f75e94ce3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5976"/><div sID="gen9097" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5976"/><hi type="bold">15. shame of ... face--</hi>blushes in disgrace. <div eID="gen9097" type="x-p"/>
entries.47af3b8a5997510b367313b06932965e9bb15ece: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5977"/><div sID="gen9098" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5977"/>16. Its cause, the taunts and presence of malignant enemies (<reference osisRef="Ps.8.2">Psa 8:2</reference>). <div eID="gen9098" type="x-p"/>
entries.c78ae5a13e34f65418c6022552306ebf30c55db4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5978"/><div sID="gen9099" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5978"/><hi type="bold">17-19. They had not apostatized totally--</hi>were still God's people. <div eID="gen9099" type="x-p"/>
entries.16a3ad71acb7ea0735004fc55e8d144ded31fdc5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5981"/><div sID="gen9104" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5981"/>20-21. A solemn appeal to God to witness their constancy.<div eID="gen9104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9105" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stretched out ... hands--</hi>gesture of worship (<reference osisRef="Exod.9.29">Ex 9:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.88.9">Psa 88:9</reference>). <div eID="gen9105" type="x-p"/>
entries.2e8cb46980320a9a4a830f36029cd8d9c0bf3252: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5982"/><div sID="gen9106" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5982"/>22. Their protracted sufferings as God's people attests the constancy. Paul (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.36">Ro 8:36</reference>) uses this to describe Christian steadfastness in persecution. <div eID="gen9106" type="x-p"/>
entries.a2e0f5e50c3d46d368b5a6208cbd2173e7192347: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5983"/><div sID="gen9107" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5983"/>23-26. This style of addressing God, as indifferent, is frequent (<reference osisRef="Ps.3.7">Psa 3:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.9.19">9:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.13.1">13:1</reference>, &c.). However low their condition, God is appealed to, on the ground, and for the honor, of His mercy. <chapter eID="Ps.44"/>

entries.c706aae65351052ac6278856fd579c1ab515627a: <div eID="gen20028" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen20029" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20030" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20030" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20029" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20031" type="x-p"/> The psalmist recounts the mercies of God; shows to his people how God in ancient times gave them the victory over all their enemies, <reference osisRef="Psa.44.1-Psa.44.8">Psa 44:1-8</reference>; points out their present miserable state, <reference osisRef="Psa.44.9-Psa.44.16">Psa 44:9-16</reference>; asserts that thy have not apostatized, and appeals to God for the truth of his assertion, <reference osisRef="Psa.44.17-Psa.44.22">Psa 44:17-22</reference>; and calls upon the Lord for deliverance from their enemies, <reference osisRef="Psa.44.23-Psa.44.26">Psa 44:23-26</reference>. <div eID="gen20031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20032" type="x-p"/> The title here is the same as that in <reference osisRef="Psa.42.1-Psa.42.11">Psa 42:1-11</reference> (note); which see. The Syriac says it was "A Psalm of the sons of Korah, which the people and Moses sung at Horeb." Such titles are fancies to which no credit should be attached. Like the preceding, it appears to belong to the time of the captivity. <div eID="gen20032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20033" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen20033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20034" type="x-p"/> We have heard with our ears - The psalmist begins with recounting the marvellous interpositions of God in behalf of the Jewish people, that he might the better strengthen his confidence, and form a ground on which to build his expectation of additional help.
entries.54f47ee5e15e069eab9309ae1d27d636b43bcbf3: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen20034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20035" type="x-p"/> Thou didst drove out the heathen - The Canaanites were as a bad tree planted in a good soil, and bringing forth bad fruit with great luxuriance. God plucked up this bad tree from the roots, and in its place planted the Hebrews as a good tree, a good vine, and caused them to take root, and fill the land.
entries.92f4e4e4e70d4dc7d7003dc727b70fad4b371050: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen20035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20036" type="x-p"/> For they got not the land - Neither by their valor, nor cunning, nor for their merit; yet, they were obliged to fight. But how did they conquer? By the right hand of the Lord, and by his arm; by his strength alone, and the light of his countenance - his favor most manifestly shown unto them.
entries.78effca8b3a8a3c04b7c94a1290e35578d6a92a3: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen20036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20037" type="x-p"/> Thou art my king - What thou wert to them, be to us. We believe in thee as they did; we have sinned and are in captivity, but we repent and turn unto thee; command, therefore, deliverances to Jacob, for we are the descendants of him in whose behalf thou hast wrought such wonders.
entries.c98e91c9ac34e793b166ed909f820c37b917f54e: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen20037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20038" type="x-p"/> Through thee will we push down - Through thy Word, במימרא bemeimra, "Thy substantial Word." - Chaldee. If thou be with us, who can be successfully against us? Literally "We will toss them in the air with our horn;" a metaphor taken from an ox or bull tossing the dogs into the air which attack him. <div eID="gen20038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20039" type="x-p"/> Through thy name - Jehovah; the infinite, the omnipotent, the eternal Being; whose power none is able to resist.
entries.d2c57bc500d0bef4baba642a5f64e8598b40bd17: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen20039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20040" type="x-p"/> I will not trust in my bow - As he is speaking of what God had already done for his forefathers, these words should be read in the past tense: "We have not trusted," etc.
entries.4d38c2b4c9955c0e88ed9e22dc1af4dd947970b7: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen20040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20041" type="x-p"/> In God we boast - We have told the heathen how great and powerful our God is. If thou do not deliver us by thy mighty power, they will not believe our report, but consider that we are held in bondage by the superior strength of their gods.
entries.db8bed6efdc72606a3c984502925a33ca917e4b2: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen20041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20042" type="x-p"/> But thou hast cast off - Our enemies have dominion over us. <div eID="gen20042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20043" type="x-p"/> And goest not forth with our armies - Were we to attempt to muster our several tribes, and form a host, like our fathers when they came out of Egypt, thou wouldst not accompany us as thou didst them: the horses and chariots of the Babylonians would soon overtake and destroy us.
entries.e85fcfa23a946b86a149e0c6fc7d2938b2d5bd16: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen20043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20044" type="x-p"/> Thou makest us to turn back - This thou didst: and our enemies, profiting by the occasion, finding our strength was departed from us, made us an easy prey, captivated our persons, and spoiled us of our property.
entries.be7e2472e34d2ccaef78c0199c4bf4467c0c7b46: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen20044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20045" type="x-p"/> And hast scattered us among the heathen - This most evidently alludes to the captivity. From the successful wars of the kings of Assyria and Chaldea against the kings of Israel and Judah, and the dispersion of the tribes under Tiglath-pileser, Shalmaneser, and Nebuchadnezzar, Jews have been found in every province of the east; there they settled, and there their successors may be found to the present day.
entries.74eb20304f83794d9687c8a62891296a4a04f1f7: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen20045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20046" type="x-p"/> Thou sellest thy people for nought - An allusion to the mode of disposing of slaves by their proprietors or sovereigns. Instead of seeking profit, thou hast made us a present to our enemies.
entries.083f37a72f5c2a920cfda129aaf2c635f33cccb9: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen20046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20047" type="x-p"/> Thou makest us a byword - We are evidently abandoned by thee, and are become so very miserable in consequence, that we are a proverb among the people: "See the Hebrews! see their misery and wretchedness! see how low the wrath of God has brought down an offending people!" And the worst curse that can be imprecated against a wicked nation is: "Mayest thou become as wretched as the Jews;" or as the old Psalter: Thou has seet us reprove til our neghburs: scornyng and hethyng til tha that er in our umgang. That es, gref, tourment that es of our neghburs, and that hethyng es noght sone gave or passand, that we suffer of tha, that er al aboute us. When men sais so byfal ye, als byfel him."
entries.a0628583dfb4577a0a7d530d31a9805eb45a9155: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen20047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20048" type="x-p"/> Yet have we not forgotten thee - These are bold words; but they must be understood in a qualified sense. We have not apostatized from thee, we have not fallen into idolatry. And this was strictly true: the charge of idolatry could never be brought against the Jewish nation from the time of the captivity, with sufficient evidence to support it.
entries.e25faf783dc3c6152b47d4e6c6f57095f439aada: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen20048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20049" type="x-p"/> Thou hast sore broken us in the place of dragons - Thou hast delivered us into the hands of a fierce, cruel, and murderous people. We, as a people, are in a similar state to one who has strayed into a wilderness, where there are no human inhabitants; who hears nothing round about him but the hissing of serpents, the howling of beasts of prey, and the terrible roaring of the lion; and who expects every moment to be devoured.
entries.37fe69a193396ee624cc6a743abf000ff8defeba: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen20049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20050" type="x-p"/> If we have forgotten the name of our God - That name, יהוה Jehovah, by which the true God was particularly distinguished, and which implied the exclusion of all other objects of adoration. <div eID="gen20050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20051" type="x-p"/> Or stretched out our hands - Made supplication; offered prayer or adoration to any strange god - a god that we had not known, nor had been acknowledged by our fathers. It has already been remarked, that from the time of the Babylonish captivity the Jews never relapsed into idolatry. It was customary among the ancients, while praying, to stretch out their hands towards the heavens, or the image they were worshipping, as if they expected to receive the favor they were asking.
entries.100ca5de8734cb3306fb60592ec4b0f1991c3f6c: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen20051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20052" type="x-p"/> Shall not God search this out? - We confidently appeal to the true Good, the searcher of hearts, for the truth of this statement.
entries.68c9ead34306dd89a4ba2eb06b7d3df4edcb2ead: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen20052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20053" type="x-p"/> For thy sake are we killed all the day long - Because of our attachment to thee and to thy religion, we are exposed to continual death; and some of us fail a daily sacrifice to the persecuting spirit of our enemies, and we all carry our lives continually in our hands. In the same state were the primitive Christians; and St. Paul applies these words to their case, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.36">Rom 8:36</reference>.
entries.e5f62a3c12a76995a422a5ec584dd2439eeb634f: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen20053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20054" type="x-p"/> A wake, why steepest thou, O Lord? - That is, Why dost thou appear as one asleep, who is regardless of the safety of his friends. This is a freedom of speech which can only be allowed to inspired men; and in their mouths it is always to be figuratively understood.
entries.af751fa44717128e8fbbb0d8104d4ce7ab3a6c7d: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen20054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20055" type="x-p"/> Wherefore hidest thou thy face - Show us the cause why thou withdrawest from us the testimony of thy approbation.
entries.01a519e35a8b765ae73000ac98399715ff47f8c4: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen20055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20056" type="x-p"/> Our soul is bowed down - Our life is drawing near to the grave. If thou delay to help us, we shall become extinct.
entries.21b7c67b823f665b13d8e6f5184775e665cda891: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen20056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20057" type="x-p"/> Arise for our help - Show forth thy power in delivering us from the hands of our enemies. <div eID="gen20057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20058" type="x-p"/> Redeem us - Ransom us from our thraldom. <div eID="gen20058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20059" type="x-p"/> For thy mercies' sake - למען חסדך lemaan chasdecha, On account of thy mercy. That we may have that proper view of thy mercy which we should have, and that we may magnify it as we ought to do, redeem us. The Vulgate has, Redime nos, propter nomen tuum, "Redeem us on account of thy name;" which the old Psalter thus paraphrases: "Help us in ryghtwysness, and by us (buy), that es, delyver us, that we be withouten drede; and al this for thi name Jehsu; noght for oure merite."  <chapter eID="Ps.44"/> <div eID="gen20059" type="x-p"/>

entries.1a96e5728b6d3881c07f279a3b96ec2daba183da: <div eID="gen9466" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">A Litany of Israel, Hard Pressed by the Enemy, and Yet Faithful to Its God</title> <div sID="gen9467" type="x-p"/> The Korahitic <hi type="italic">Maskı̂l</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.42.1-Ps.42.11">Psa 42:1-11</reference>, with its counterpart <reference osisRef="Ps.43.1-Ps.43.5">Psa 43:1-5</reference>, if followed by a second, to which a place is here assigned by manifold accords with Ps 42-43, viz., with its complaints (cf. PsPsa 44:26 with the refrain of <reference osisRef="Ps.43.1-Ps.43.5">Psa 43:1-5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.42.1-Ps.42.11">Psa 42:1-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.44.10">Psa 44:10</reference>, Psa 44:24. with <reference osisRef="Ps.43.2">Psa 43:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.42.10">Psa 42:10</reference>), and prayers (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.44.5">Psa 44:5</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.43.3">Psa 43:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.42.9">Psa 42:9</reference>). The counterpart to this Psalm is <reference osisRef="Ps.85.1">Psa 85:1</reference>-13. Just as Ps 42-43 and <reference osisRef="Ps.84.1-Ps.84.12">Psa 84:1-12</reference> form a pair, so do Ps 44 and <reference osisRef="Ps.85.1-Ps.85.13">Psa 85:1-13</reference> as being Korahitic plaintive and supplicatory Psalms of a national character. Moreover, <reference osisRef="Ps.60.1-Ps.60.12">Psa 60:1-12</reference> by David, Ps 80 by Asaph, and Ps 89 by Ethan, are nearest akin to it. In all these three there are similar lamentations over the present as contrasting with the former times and with the promise of God; but they do not contain any like expression of consciousness of innocence, a feature in which Ps 44 has no equal. <div eID="gen9467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9468" type="x-p"/> In this respect the Psalm seems to be most satisfactorily explained by the situation of the חסידים (saints), who under the leadership of the Maccabees defended their nationality and their religion against the Syrians and fell as martyrs by thousands. The war of that period was, in its first beginnings at least, a holy war of religion; and the nation which then went forth on the side of Jahve against Jupiter Olympius, was really, in distinction from the apostates, a people true to its faith and confession, which had to lament over God’s doom of wrath in 1 Macc. 1:64, just as in this Psalm. There is even a tradition that it was a stated lamentation Psalm of the time of the Maccabees. The Levites daily ascended the pulpit (דוכן) and raised the cry of prayer: Awake, why sleepest Thou, O Lord?! These Levite criers praying for the interposition of God were called מעוררים (wakers). It is related in <hi type="italic">B. Sota 48a</hi> of Jochanan the high priest, i.e., John Hyrcanus (135-107 b.c.), that he put an end to these מעוררים, saying to them: “Doth the Deity sleep? Hath not the Scripture said: Behold the Keeper of Israel slumbereth not and sleepeth not!? Only in a time when Israel was in distress and the peoples of the world in rest and prosperity, only in reference to such circumstances was it said: Awake, why sleepest Thou, O Lord?” <div eID="gen9468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9469" type="x-p"/> Nevertheless many considerations are opposed to the composition of the Psalm in the time of the Maccabees. We will mention only a few. In the time of the Maccabees the nation did not exactly suffer any overthrow of its “armies” (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.10">Psa 44:10</reference>) after having gathered up its courage: the arms of Judah, of Jonathan, and of Simon were victorious, and the one defeat to which Hitzig refers the Psalm, viz., the defeat of Joseph and Azaria against Gorgias in Jamnia (1 Macc. 5:55ff.), was a punishment brought upon themselves by an indiscreet enterprise. The complaints in Psa 44:10. are therefore only partially explained by the evmnts of that time; and since a nation is a unit and involved as a whole, it is also surprising that no mention whatever is made of the apostates. But Ewald’s reference of the Psalm to the time of the post-exilic Jerusalem is still more inadmissible; and when, in connection with this view, the question is asked, What disaster of war is then intended? no answer can be given; and the reference to the time of Jehoiachin, which Tholuck in vain endeavours to set in a more favourable light - a king who did evil in the eyes of Jahve, <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.9">2Ch 36:9</reference>, with which the descriptions of character drawn by Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.20-Jer.22.30">Jer 22:20-30</reference>, and by Ezekiel, <reference osisRef="Ezek.19.1-Ezek.19.14">Eze 19:1-14</reference>, fully accord - is also inadmissible. On the other hand, the position of the Psalm in the immediate neighbourhood of Psalms belonging to the time of Jehoshaphat, and also to a certain extent its contents, favours the early part of the reign of king Joash, in which, as becomes evident from the prophecy of Joel, there was no idolatry on the part of the people to be punished, and yet there were severe afflictions of the people to be bewailed. It was then not long since the Philistines and Arabs from the neighbourhood of the Cushites had broken in upon Judah, ransacked Jerusalem and sold the captive people of Judah for a mere song to the Greeks (2Ch 21:16., <reference osisRef="Joel.3.2-Joel.3.8">Joe 3:2-8</reference>). But this reference to contemporary history is also untenable. That unhappy event, together with others, belongs to the category of well-merited judgments, which came upon king and people in the reign of Jehoram; nor does the Psalm sound like a retrospective glance at the time of Jehoram from the standpoint of the time of Joash: the defeat of which it complains, is one that is now only just experienced. <div eID="gen9469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9470" type="x-p"/> Thus we seem consequently driven back to the time of David; and the question arises, whether the Psalm does not admit, with <reference osisRef="Ps.60.1-Ps.60.12">Psa 60:1-12</reference>, with which it forms a twin couple, of being understood as the offspring of a similar situation, viz., of the events which resulted from the Syro-Ammonitish war. The fact that a conflict with the foes of the kingdom in the south, viz., with the Edomites, was also mixed up with the wars with the Ammonites and their Syrian allies at that period, becomes evident from Psa 60:1. when compared with <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.13">2Sa 8:13</reference>, where the words ἐπάταξε τὴν Ἰδουμαίαν (lxx) have fallen out. Whilst David was contending with the Syrians, the Edomites came down upon the country that was denuded of troops. And from 1Ki 11:15 it is very evident that they then caused great bloodshed; for, according to that passage, Joab buried the slain and took fearful revenge upon the Edomites: he marched, after having slain them in the Valley of Salt, into Idumaea and there smote every male. Perhaps, with Hengstenberg, Keil, and others, the Psalm is to be explained from the position of Israel before this overthrow of the Edomites. The fact that in <reference osisRef="Ps.44.12">Psa 44:12</reference> the nation complains of a dispersion among the heathen may be understood by means of a deduction from <reference osisRef="Amos.1.6">Amo 1:6</reference>, according to which the Edomites had carried on a traffic in captive Israelites. And the lofty self-consciousness, which finds expression in the Psalm, is after all best explained by the times of David; for these and the early part of the times of Solomon are the only period in the history of Israel when the nation as a whole could boast of being free and pure of all foreign influence in its worship. In the kindred Psa 60:1-12; 80 (also Ps 89), it is true this self-consciousness does not attain the same lofty expression in this respect Ps 40 stands perfectly alone: it is like the national mirroring of the Book of Job, and by reason of this takes a unique position in the range of Old Testament literature side by side with Lam. 3 and the deutero-Isaiah. Israel’s affliction, which could not possibly be of a punitive character, resembles the affliction of Job; in this Psalm, Israel stands in exactly the same relation to God as Job and the “Servant of Jahve” in Isaiah, if we except all that was desponding in Job’s complaint and all that was expiatory in the affliction of the Servant of Jahve. But this very self-consciousness does somewhat approximately find expression even in Psa 60:4. In that passage also no distinction is made between Israel and the God-fearing ones, and the battle, in which Israel is defeated, but not without hope of final victory, is a battle for the truth. <div eID="gen9470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9471" type="x-p"/> The charge has been brought against this Psalm, that it manifests a very superficial apprehension of the nature of sin, in consequence of which the writer has been betrayed into accusing God of unfaithfulness, instead of seeking for guilt in the congregation of Israel. This judgment is unjust. The writer certainly cannot mean to disown the sins of individuals, nor even this or that transgression of the whole people. but any apostasy on the part of the nation from its God, such as could account for its rejection, did not exist at that time. The supremacy granted to the heathen over Israel is, therefore, an abnormal state of things, and for this very reason the poet, on the ground of Israel’s fidelity and of God’s loving-kindness, prays for speedy deliverance. A Psalm born directly out of the heart of the New Testament church would certainly sound very differently. For the New Testament church is not a national community; and both as regards the relation between the reality and idea of the church, and as regards the relation between its afflictions and the motive and design of God, the view of the New Testament church penetrates far deeper. It knows that it is God’s love that makes it conformable to the passion of Christ, in order that, being crucified unto the world, it may become through suffering partaker of the glory of its Lord and Head. <div eID="gen9471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9472" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ps.44.1-Ps.44.3">Psa 44:1-3</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_44:2-4) The poet opens with a tradition coming down from the time of Moses and of Joshua which they have heard with their own ears, in order to demonstrate the vast distance between the character of the former times and the present, just as Asaph, also, in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.3">Psa 78:3</reference>, appeals not to the written but to the spoken word. That which has been heard follows in the <hi type="italic">oratio directa</hi>. <reference osisRef="Ps.44.3">Psa 44:3</reference> explains what kind of “work” is intended: it is the granting of victory over the peoples of Canaan, the work of God for which Moses prays in Psa 90:16. Concerning ידך, vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.3.5">Psa 3:5</reference>; Psa 17:14. The position of the words here, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.69.11">Psa 69:11</reference>; 83:19, leads one to suppose that ידך is treated as a permutative of אתּה, and consequently in the same case with it. The figure of “planting” (after <reference osisRef="Exod.15.17">Exo 15:17</reference>) is carried forward in ותּשׁלּחם; for this word means to send forth far away, to make wide-branching, a figure which is wrought up in Ps 80. It was not Israel’s own work, but (כּי, no indeed, for [Germ. <hi type="italic">nein, denn</hi>]<hi type="italic">= imo</hi>) God’s work: “Thy right hand and Thine arm and the light of Thy countenance,” they it was which brought Israel salvation, i.e., victory. The combination of synonyms ימינך וּזרועך is just as in <reference osisRef="Ps.74.11">Psa 74:11</reference>, Sir. 33:7, χείρα καὶ βραχίονα δεξιόν, and is explained by both the names of the members of the body as applied to God being only figures: the right hand being a figure for energetic interposition, and the arm for an effectual power that carries through the thing designed (cf. e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.77.16">Psa 77:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.53.1">Psa 53:1</reference>), just as the light of His countenance is a figure for His loving-kindness which lights up all darkness. The final cause was His purpose of love: for (inasmuch as) Thou wast favourable to them (רצה as in <reference osisRef="Ps.85.2">Psa 85:2</reference>). The very same thought, viz., that Israel owes the possession of Canaan to nothing but Jahve’s free grace, runs all through Deut. 9.
entries.522de6dba7d32f04ae342092bbabd7bef54dd809: <reference osisRef="Ps.44.4-Ps.44.8">Psa 44:4-8</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_44:5-9) Out of the retrospective glance at the past, so rich in mercy springs up (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.5">Psa 44:5</reference>) the confident prayer concerning the present, based upon the fact of the theocratic relationship which began in the time of the deliverance wrought under Moses (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.5">Deu 33:5</reference>). In the substantival clause אתּה הוּא מלכּי, הוּא is neither logical copula nor predicate (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.102.28">Psa 102:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.39">Deu 32:39</reference>, there equivalent to אתּה הוּא אשׁר, cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.21.17">1Ch 21:17</reference>), but an expressive resumption of the subject, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.43.25">Isa 43:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.12">Jer 49:12</reference>; Neh 9:6., Ezr 5:11, and in the frequently recurring expression יהוה הוא האלהים; it is therefore to be rendered: Thou-He who (such an one) is my King. May He therefore, by virtue of His duty as king which He has voluntarily taken upon Himself, and of the kingly authority and power indwelling in Him, command the salvation of Jacob, full and entire (Ps 18:51; 53:7). צוּה as in Psa 42:9. <hi type="italic">Jacob</hi> is used for <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> just as <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi> is used instead of <hi type="italic">Jahve</hi>. If Elohim, Jacob’s King, now turns graciously to His people, they will again be victorious and invincible, as <reference osisRef="Ps.44.6">Psa 44:6</reference> affirms. נגּח with reference to קרן as a figure and emblem of strength, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.89.25">Psa 89:25</reference> and frequently; קמינוּ equivalent to קמים עלינוּ. But only in the strength of God (בּך as in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.30">Psa 18:30</reference>); for not in my bow do I trust, etc., Psa 44:7. This teaching Israel has gathered from the history of the former times; there is no bidding defiance with the bow and sword and all the carnal weapons of attack, but Thou, etc., Psa 44:8. This “Thou” in הושׁעתּנוּ is the emphatic word; the preterites describe facts of experience belonging to history. It is not Israel’s own might that gives them the supremacy, but God’s gracious might in Israel’s weakness. Elohim is, therefore, Israel’s glory or pride: “In Elohim do we praise,” i.e., we glory or make our boast in Him; cf. הלּל על, Psa 10:3. The music here joins in after the manner of a hymn. The Psalm here soars aloft to the more joyous height of praise, from which it now falls abruptly into bitter complaint.
entries.28327a6b14658df9958621a877f1e87549ebaab2: <reference osisRef="Ps.44.9-Ps.44.12">Psa 44:9-12</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_44:10-13) Just as אף signifies <hi type="italic">imo vero</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.58.3">Psa 58:3</reference>) when it comes after an antecedent clause that is expressly or virtually a negative, it may mean “nevertheless, ho'moos,” when it opposes a contrastive to an affirmative assertion, as is very frequently the case with גּם or וגם. True, it does not mean this in itself, but in virtue of its logical relation: we praise Thee, we celebrate Thy name unceasingly - also (= nevertheless) Thou hast cast off. From this point the Psalm comes into closest connection with <reference osisRef="Ps.89.39">Psa 89:39</reference>, on a still more extended scale, however, with <reference osisRef="Ps.60.1-Ps.60.12">Psa 60:1-12</reference>, which dates from the time of the Syro-Ammonitish war, in which Psalm <reference osisRef="Ps.44.10">Psa 44:10</reference> recurs almost word for word. The צבאות are not exactly standing armies (an objection which has been raised against the Maccabean explanation), they are the hosts of the people that are drafted into battle, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.12.41">Exo 12:41</reference>, the hosts that went forth out of Egypt. Instead of leading these to victory as their victorious Captain (<reference osisRef="2Sam.5.24">2Sa 5:24</reference>), God leaves them to themselves and allows them to be smitten by the enemy. The enemy spoil למו, i.e., just as they like, without meeting with any resistance, to their hearts’ content. And whilst He gives over (נתן as in Mic 5:2, and the first יתּן in <reference osisRef="Isa.41.2">Isa 41:2</reference>) one portion of the people as “sheep appointed for food,” another becomes a <hi type="italic">diaspora</hi> or dispersion among the heathen, viz., by being sold to them as slaves, and that בּלא־הון, “for not-riches,” i.e., for a very low price, a mere nothing. We see from <reference osisRef="Joel.3.3">Joe 3:3</reference> in what way this is intended. The form of the litotes is continued in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.44.13">Psa 44:13</reference></hi>: Thou didst not go high in the matter of their purchase-money; the rendering of Maurer is correct: <hi type="italic">in statuendis pretiis eorum</hi>. The ב is in this instance not the <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> of the price as in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.44.13">Psa 44:13</reference></hi>, but, as in the phrase הלּל בּ, the <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> of the sphere and thereby indirectly of the object. רבּה in the sense of the Aramaic רבּי (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.22.16">Pro 22:16</reference>, and the derivatives תּרבּית, מרבּית), to make a profit, to practise usury (Hupfeld), produces a though that is unworthy of God; vid., on the other hand, Isa 52:3. At the heads of the strophe stands (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.44.10">Psa 44:10</reference></hi>) a perfect with an aorist following: ולא תצא is consequently a negative ותּצא. And <reference osisRef="Ps.44.18">Psa 44:18</reference>, which sums up the whole, shows that all the rest is also intended to be retrospective.
entries.0bf0dc5b4349d48d52f3e88ce86e4564e9247233: <reference osisRef="Ps.44.13-Ps.44.16">Psa 44:13-16</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_44:14-17) To this defeat is now also added the shame that springs out of it. A distinction is made between the neighbouring nations, or those countries lying immediately round about Israel (סביבות, as in the exactly similar passage <reference osisRef="Ps.79.4">Psa 79:4</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.80.7">Psa 80:7</reference>, which closely resembles it), and the nations of the earth that dwell farther away from Israel. משׁל is here a jesting, taunting proverb, and one that holds Israel up as an example of a nation undergoing chastisement (vid., <reference osisRef="Hab.2.6">Hab 2:6</reference>). The shaking of the head is, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.22.8">Psa 22:8</reference>, a gesture of malicious astonishment. In נגדּי תּמיד (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.38.18">Psa 38:18</reference>) we have both the permanent aspect or look and the perpetual consciousness. Instead of “shame covers my face,” the expression is “the shame of my face covers me,” i.e., it has overwhelmed my entire inward and outward being (cf. concerning the radical notions of בּושׁ, Ps 6:11, and חפר, <reference osisRef="Ps.34.6">Psa 34:6</reference>). The juxtaposition of “enemy and revengeful man” has its origin in Psa 8:3. In <reference osisRef="Ps.44.17">Psa 44:17</reference> מקּול and מפּני alternate; the former is used of the impression made by the jeering voice, the other of the impression produced by the enraged mien.
entries.dd52ec008dc1bc6e02b728d780ac9dc01248251b: <reference osisRef="Ps.44.17-Ps.44.21">Psa 44:17-21</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_44:18-22) If Israel compares its conduct towards God with this its lot, it cannot possibly regard it as a punishment that it has justly incurred. Construed with the accusative, בּוא signifies, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.35.8">Psa 35:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.36.12">Psa 36:12</reference>, to come upon one, and more especially of an evil lot and of powers that are hostile. שׁקּר, to lie or deceive, with בּ of the object on whom the deception or treachery is practised, as in Psa 89:34. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.44.19">Psa 44:19</reference></hi> אשּׁוּר is construed as <hi type="italic">fem</hi>., exactly as in <reference osisRef="Job.31.8">Job 31:8</reference>; the <hi type="italic">fut. consec</hi>. is also intended as such (as e.g., in <reference osisRef="Job.3.10">Job 3:10</reference>; Num 16:14): that our step should have declined from, etc.; inward apostasy is followed by outward wandering and downfall. This is therefore not one of the many instances in which the לא of one clause also has influence over the clause that follows (Ges. §152, 3). כּי, <reference osisRef="Ps.44.20">Psa 44:20</reference>, has the sense of <hi type="italic">quod</hi>: we have not revolted against Thee, that Thou shouldest on that account have done to us the thing which is now befallen us. Concerning תּנּיּם vid., Isa 13:22. A “place of jackals” is, like a habitation of dragons (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.22">Jer 10:22</reference>), the most lonesome and terrible wilderness; the place chosen was, according to this, an inhospitable מדבר, far removed from the dwellings of men. כּסּה is construed with על of the person covered, and with בּ of that with which (<reference osisRef="1Sam.19.13">1Sa 19:13</reference>) he is covered: Thou coveredst us over with deepest darkness (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.23.4">Psa 23:4</reference>). אם, <reference osisRef="Ps.44.21">Psa 44:21</reference>, is not that of asseveration (verily we have not forgotten), but, as the interrogatory apodosis <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.44.22">Psa 44:22</reference></hi> shows, conditional: if we have (= should have) forgotten. This would not remain hidden from Him who knoweth the heart, for the secrets of men’s hearts are known to Him. Both the form and matter here again strongly remind one of Job 31, more especially <reference osisRef="Job.31.4">Job 31:4</reference>; cf. also on תּעלמות, <reference osisRef="Job.11.6">Job 11:6</reference>; Job 28:11.
entries.9dfe963afb92aeed8a99d4d7dc19d869a2ee38fa: <reference osisRef="Ps.44.22-Ps.44.26">Psa 44:22-26</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_44:23-27) The church is not conscious of any apostasy, for on the contrary it is suffering for the sake of its fidelity. Such is the meaning intended by כּי, <reference osisRef="Ps.44.23">Psa 44:23</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.37.20">Psa 37:20</reference>). The emphasis lies on עליך, which is used exactly as in Psa 69:8. Paul, in <reference osisRef="Rom.8.36">Rom 8:36</reference>, transfers this utterance to the sufferings of the New Testament church borne in witnessing for the truth, or I should rather say he considers it as a divine utterance corresponding as it were prophetically to the sufferings of the New Testament church, and by anticipation, coined concerning it and for its use, inasmuch as he cites it with the words καθὼς γέγραπται. The suppliant cries עוּרה and הקיצה are Davidic, and found in his earlier Ps; <reference osisRef="Ps.7.7">Psa 7:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.35.23">Psa 35:23</reference>; Psa 59:5., cf. Psa 78:65. God is said to sleep when He does not interpose in whatever is taking place in the outward world here below; for the very nature of sleep is a turning in into one’s own self from all relationship to the outer world, and a resting of the powers which act outwardly. The writer of our Psalm is fond of couplets of synonyms like ענינוּ ולחצנוּ in <reference osisRef="Ps.44.25">Psa 44:25</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.44.4">Psa 44:4</reference>, ימינך וּזרועך. <reference osisRef="Ps.119.25">Psa 119:25</reference> is an echo of Psa 44:26. The suppliant cry קוּמה (in this instance in connection with the עזרתה which follows, it is to be accented on the <hi type="italic">ultima</hi>) is Davidic, <reference osisRef="Ps.3.8">Psa 3:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.7.7">Psa 7:7</reference>; but originally it is Mosaic. Concerning the <hi type="italic">ah</hi> of עזרתה, here as also in <reference osisRef="Ps.63.8">Psa 63:8</reference> of like meaning with לעזרתי, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.20">Psa 22:20</reference>, and frequently, vid., on Psa 3:3. Marriage Song in Honour of the Peerless King <div eID="gen9472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9473" type="x-p"/> To a Korahitic <hi type="italic">Maskı̂l</hi>  is appended a song of the same name, and likewise bearing a royal impress after the style of the Korahitic productions. But whilst in <reference osisRef="Ps.44.5">Psa 44:5</reference> the <hi type="italic">words “Thou, Thou art my King, Elohim,”</hi> are addressed in prayer to the God of Israel, in this Psalm the person of the king who is celebrated is a matter of doubt and controversy. The Epistle to the Hebrews (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.8">Heb 1:8</reference>) proceeds on the assumption that it is the future Christ, the Son of God. It is supported in this view by a tradition of the ancient synagogue, in accordance with which the Targumist renders <reference osisRef="Ps.45.3">Psa 45:3</reference>, <hi type="italic">“Thy beauty, O King Messiah, is greater than that of the children of men.”</hi> This Messianic interpretation must be very ancient. Just as <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.32">Eze 21:32</reference> refers back to שׁילה, <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen 49:10</reference>, גּבּור אל among the names of the Messiah in <reference osisRef="Isa.9.5">Isa 9:5</reference> (cf. Zec 12:8) refers back in a similar manner to Ps 45. And whilst the reception of the Song of Songs into the canon admits of being understood even without the assumption of any prophetically allegorical meaning in it, the reception of this Psalm without any such assumption is unintelligible. But this prophetically Messianic sense is therefore not the original meaning of the Psalm. The Psalm is a poem composed for some special occasion the motive of which is some contemporary event. The king whom it celebrates was a contemporary of the poet. If, however, it was a king belonging to David’s family, then he was a possessor of a kingship to which were attached, according to 2 Sam. 7, great promises extending into the unlimited future, and on which, consequently, hung all the prospects of the future prosperity and glory of Israel; and the poet is therefore fully warranted in regarding him in the light of the Messianic idea, and the church is also fully warranted in referring the song, which took its rise in some passing occasion, as a song for all ages, to the great King of the future, the goal of its hope. Moreover, we find only such poems of an occasional and individual character received into the Psalter, as were adapted to remain in constant use by the church as prayers and spiritual songs. <div eID="gen9473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9474" type="x-p"/> With respect to the historical occasion of the song, we adhere to the conjecture advanced in our commentary on Canticles and on the Epistle to the Hebrews, viz., that it was composed in connection with the marriage of Joram of Judah with Athaliah. The reference to the marriage of Ahab of Israel with Jezebel of Tyre, set forth by Hitzig, is at once set aside by the fact that the poet idealizes the person celebrated, as foreshadowing the Messiah, in a way that can only be justified in connection with a <hi type="italic">Davidic</hi> king. It could more readily be Solomon the king of Israel, whose appearance was fair as that of a woman, but majestic as that of a hero.<note placement="foot">So Disraeli in his romance of <hi type="italic">Alroy</hi> (1845).</note> <div eID="gen9474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9475" type="x-p"/> Even to the present day several interpreters<note placement="foot">So even Kurtz in the <hi type="italic">Dorpater Zeitschrift</hi> for 1865, S. 1-24.</note> explain the Psalm of Solomon’s marriage with the daughter of Pharaoh; but the entire absence of any mention of Egypt is decisive against this view. Hence Hupfeld imagines a daughter of Hiram to be the bride, by reference to the Zidonian Ashtôreth which is mentioned among Solomon’s strange gods (1Ki 11:5, 1Ki 11:33). But the fact that the king here celebrated is called upon to go forth to battle, is also strange, whilst the glory of Solomon consists in his being, in accordance with his name, the Prince of Peace, or אישׁ מנוּחה, 1Ch 22:9. Further, the wish is expressed for him that he may have children who shall take the place of his ancestors: Solomon, however, had a royal father, but not royal fathers; and there is the less ground for any retrospective reference to the princes of Judah as Solomon’s ancestors (which Kurtz inclines to), since of these only one, viz., Nahshon, occurs among the ancestry of David. <div eID="gen9475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9476" type="x-p"/> All this speaks against Solomon, but just with equal force in favour of Joram, as being the king celebrated. This Joram is the son of Jehoshaphat, the second Solomon of the Israelitish history. He became king even during the lifetime of his pious father, under whom the Salomonic prosperity of Israel was revived (cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.1">2Ch 18:1</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.21.3">Psa 21:3</reference>, 2Ki 8:16, and Winer’s <hi type="italic">Realwörterbuch</hi> under <hi type="italic">Jehoram</hi>); he was also married to Athaliah during his father’s lifetime; and it is natural, that just at that time, when Judah had again attained to the height of the glory of the days of Solomon, the highest hopes should be gathered around these nuptials.
